name: TB-500
evidenceNote: No human trial of the TB-500 fragment has been published, and the FDA says it has found no human exposure data. The healing claims borrow from animal work and a few small trials of the full-length protein, a different molecule.
summary: TB-500 is a synthetic piece of thymosin beta-4 sold for injury recovery. It is unapproved, untested in people, and banned in sport.
keyTakeaway: TB-500 is a short synthetic peptide, usually the seven-amino-acid piece of thymosin beta-4 that binds actin, sold for muscle, tendon, and wound recovery. No human trial of the fragment exists; the claims are borrowed from animal studies and small trials of the much larger full-length protein. It is not FDA-approved. In July 2026 an FDA advisory committee voted 8 to 6 to back compounding it, against the advice of FDA scientists, and since October 28, 2026 federal policy lets licensed pharmacies compound it while rulemaking is pending. WADA bans it at all times.

blocks.text: TB-500 is a product name, not a drug name. It refers to synthetic peptides sold for recovery from muscle, tendon, and ligament injuries, and anti-doping labs have long suspected its use in sport. When a Belgian anti-doping lab analyzed a TB-500 product, the active ingredient was a seven-amino-acid sequence (Ac-LKKTETQ), the acetylated 17 to 23 stretch of the natural protein thymosin beta-4 [2]. The FDA's own listing describes TB-500 the same way [3].

Thymosin beta-4 itself is a much larger natural protein that platelets, macrophages, and many other cell types release after an injury [1]. The fragment is a small part of it. Because labeling in this market is loose, a vial sold as TB-500 may contain the short fragment, the full protein, or something else entirely.

The proposed mechanism comes from the parent protein. Thymosin beta-4 binds actin, the protein that forms each cell's internal skeleton, and that binding helps cells move. In animal and lab studies, the full protein drew stem and progenitor cells into damaged tissue, encouraged new blood vessels, calmed inflammation, and reduced scarring in skin, eye, heart, and brain injury models [1].

The fragment in TB-500 contains the actin-binding motif, so sellers assume it carries the same benefits. That assumption has not been tested in people. The fragment is far shorter than the protein, may be broken down differently, and has been studied much less. Mechanism data on the full protein are a reason to study the fragment, not evidence that it works.

No. TB-500 is not approved for any use, and no company has filed it as a new drug. What changed in 2026 is its position with compounding pharmacies, which make drugs for individual patients from bulk ingredients.

The FDA's safety page lists the fragment among nominations that were withdrawn in April 2026 and notes that the agency has found no human exposure data and lacks key safety information [3]. On July 23, 2026, the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee voted 8 to 6, with one abstention, to recommend adding TB-500 to the 503A bulks list for wound healing. FDA scientists had recommended against it, citing safety, efficacy, and characterization concerns [4][10]. On October 28, 2026, HHS announced it would not take action against licensed pharmacies and physicians compounding six peptides, TB-500 among them, while formal rulemaking proceeds [9]. The policy requires the ingredient to come from an FDA-registered facility with a certificate of analysis and asks compounders to report serious adverse events [5].

Enforcement discretion is not approval. It does not mean the FDA found TB-500 safe or effective, and it has no stated end date. In sport, the WADA list bans thymosin beta-4 and its derivatives, naming TB-500 as an example, in and out of competition [8].

blocks.text: For the TB-500 fragment, there is no published human trial of benefit or safety. Everything sold under the name rests on research into the full-length protein, and even that human evidence is thin.

rows: Topical full-length thymosin beta-4 at rising doses in 72 planned patients
Built to measure safety and tolerability; still enrolling when reported [6]
0.1% full-length thymosin beta-4 drops in 18 people with neurotrophic keratopathy
6 of 10 healed at 4 weeks vs 1 of 8 on placebo, a trend that missed significance (p = 0.0656) [7]

blocks.text: The two human studies shown both used the whole protein, applied to skin or eyes rather than injected, and both were small. The eye-drop trial was designed and funded by the company developing the product [7]. They are early signals about the full protein in specific wounds, not evidence about a seven-amino-acid fragment injected for sports injuries.
So the recovery claims attached to TB-500 have not been shown in people. Questions about dose, purity, how long the fragment lasts in the body, and long-term effects remain unanswered.

sections.heading: How is TB-500 different from thymosin beta-4?

blocks.text: Thymosin beta-4 is the full-length natural protein, and it is the version that has reached small clinical trials for corneal and skin wounds [6][7]. TB-500 is a seven-amino-acid synthetic piece of it [2]. Regulators treat them separately: the 2026 compounding votes and the HHS policy name TB-500, the fragment, not the full protein [4][5]. Anti-doping rules, by contrast, ban both [8].
